title: Vayelech: write this song (Deuteronomy 31:19)
hook: the Torah's last command is to write it; the Talmud says each Jew should write a scroll (Sanhedrin 21b)

segments.voice: Yesterday, hakhel: everyone gathering once in seven years. Your line was everyone gathers. Who did you invite to learn? Today, the last commandment, and it involves a pen. Day five hundred twenty-five.

When did you last write something out by hand that you didn't have to? Not a signature, not a shopping list. Just copying words because they mattered. A pen slows you down, and slowing down changes what you notice. You can't skim with a pen. Every letter gets a moment. Almost at its end, the Torah gives a commandment about writing. By the traditional count, it's the last commandment in the whole Torah.
screen: `NOT A SIGNATURE, NOT A LIST.` → `YOU CAN'T SKIM WITH A PEN.` → `THE LAST COMMANDMENT.`

segments.voice: God tells Moses: "Now therefore write ye this song for you, and teach thou it the children of Israel." Plainly, the song is the poem that comes next, Ha'azinu, which we'll begin in two days. But the rabbis read the verse more widely. The song, they said, means the whole Torah. And write ye means every person. In the Talmud, in Sanhedrin, the teacher Rabbah says: even if your parents left you a Torah scroll, it's a commandment to write one of your own. Maimonides counts this among the six hundred thirteen commandments, and in the Torah's order it comes last. Writing a full scroll by hand takes a trained scribe, a sofer, many months of work. So how does an ordinary person do it? Some commission a scribe. In many communities, when a new scroll is nearly finished, people each take a turn completing a letter, with the scribe guiding the hand. And some authorities, like the medieval sage known as the Rosh, taught that in later times writing or acquiring books of Torah study carries the same spirit. Underneath is a striking idea. Inheriting isn't enough. The tradition wants each person to make it their own, letter by letter. This week we walked from Nitzavim into Vayelech. You can return. Very near. Choose life. He went to them. Strong and of good courage. Everyone gathers. And now: write your own.
screen: `WRITE YE THIS SONG.` · `RABBAH: WRITE YOUR OWN SCROLL.` · `THE LAST OF THE 613.` · `ONE LETTER, GUIDED BY THE SCRIBE.` · then, large: `WRITE YOUR OWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: copy out one verse by hand. If you can, find a pen and paper. If not, trace the letters with a finger on your palm or on the table. Choose a line that's stayed with you this month. Maybe choose life, or the word is very nigh unto thee. Copy it slowly, one letter at a time. Notice where your hand hesitates. Notice a word you'd never really looked at before. The bell holds the time.
Vayelech. And he went. And in it, the last commandment: write this song. Write your own.
Your line: write your own. Today, copy one line that matters to you by hand, and keep it somewhere you'll see it. Day five hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: A Torah scroll is written by hand by a trained scribe (sofer) on parchment; many communities celebrate the completion of a new scroll by letting members fill in its final letters, guided by the scribe.

notes: Deuteronomy 31:19 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Sanhedrin 21b (Rabbah): even if one's ancestors left a scroll, it is a mitzvah to write one's own. Paraphrased.
'Last of the 613 in the Torah's order' is the common Sefer HaChinuch ordering (mitzvah 613); confirm phrasing with Maimonides' count.
Rosh, Hilchot Sefer Torah 1: in later generations the mitzvah extends to writing books of Chumash, Mishnah, Talmud and commentaries. Paraphrased.
